full_text_en:
Guiding Case No. 239

Wang v. Beijing Mou Culture Media Co., Ltd. — labor dispute

(Discussed and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, published on December 20, 2024)

Keywords: Civil / Labor dispute / Confirmation of labor relationship / New forms of employment / Network anchor / Agency contract / No labor relationship exists

Ruling Gist

Where an agency company does not exercise strong control over the working hours, work content, or work process of a practitioner, the practitioner is not required to strictly comply with the company's labor management rules, and the practitioner has relatively strong bargaining power over matters such as profit distribution, it shall be determined that no dominant labor management exists between the parties and that no labor relationship exists.

Basic Facts

Wang was a network anchor who created and operated a self-media account on an online platform. In March 2020, Wang entered into an Exclusive Agency Contract with Beijing Mou Culture Media Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Beijing Mou Media Company). The contract stipulated: Wang authorized Beijing Mou Media Company to exclusively provide agency services and business operations related to text, audio, and video matters on self-media platforms; Wang's primary income was derived from monthly transaction amounts, with a guaranteed minimum fee and commission determined based on the monthly transaction amount; Beijing Mou Media Company would deduct necessary expenses from the revenue and then distribute the remainder between the parties in proportion; Wang had the right to raise objections regarding the settlement of revenue distribution; Wang was required to arrive at the workplace on time as arranged by Beijing Mou Media Company and complete the work tasks as agreed; the contract was a cooperative service contract, not a labor contract, and the parties did not establish a labor relationship by entering into this contract. During the contract formation process, Wang specifically modified the revenue distribution provisions in his favor.

In the actual performance of the contract, Wang operated his self-media account in accordance with the agreement between the parties. His monthly income was not fixed and depended on the platform advertising revenue generated from their cooperative operations. After the contract was signed, Wang's self-media account was jointly operated and managed by Wang and Beijing Mou Media Company, and the number of followers grew from nearly one million before signing to four million. Additionally, Wang participated in activities such as advertising production and publication, as well as variety show performances, as recommended by Beijing Mou Media Company.

Subsequently, a dispute arose between the parties. Wang applied for labor arbitration, requesting confirmation of the existence of a labor relationship with Beijing Mou Media Company from March 1, 2020 to April 13, 2021, and payment of a bonus of RMB 255,217.5 (currency unit: RMB, the same below) from February 1, 2021 to April 13, 2021, as well as a double-wage difference of RMB 110,000 for failure to conclude a written labor contract from March 1, 2020 to February 28, 2021. The Beijing Chaoyang District Labor and Personnel Dispute Arbitration Commission ruled to dismiss all of Wang's arbitration requests. Wang refused to accept the decision and filed a lawsuit with the Beijing Chaoyang District People's Court.

Judgment

The Beijing Chaoyang District People's Court rendered a civil judgment (No. (2022) Jing 0105 Min Chu 9090) on November 25, 2022, dismissing Wang's claims. After the judgment was pronounced, Wang refused to accept it and appealed. The Beijing Third Intermediate People's Court rendered a civil judgment (No. (2023) Jing 03 Min Zhong 7051) on September 5, 2023, dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment.

Reasoning

The focus of the dispute in this case is: whether a labor relationship exists between Beijing Mou Media Company and its network anchor Wang.

The essential characteristic of a labor relationship is dominant labor management, i.e., the existence of strong personal subordination, economic subordination, and organizational subordination between the worker and the employer. Under new forms of employment, the legal relationship between an enterprise and a network anchor must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis, focusing on examining the content of the rights and obligations between the enterprise and the network anchor and the manner in which they are determined, accurately distinguishing between performance requirements arising from an agency relationship and labor management, and determining whether the platform enterprise exercises dominant labor management over the network anchor and whether a labor relationship exists between them.

In this case, based on the contract entered into by the parties and the actual performance circumstances, Beijing Mou Media Company did not exercise dominant labor management over network anchor Wang. Specifically: First, under the agency contract entered into by Beijing Mou Media Company and Wang, Wang was required to arrive at the workplace on time as arranged by Beijing Mou Media Company and complete work tasks as agreed. However, Wang was not required to comply with Beijing Mou Media Company's work rules, labor discipline, or reward and punishment measures. Therefore, although Beijing Mou Media Company could impose necessary restrictions on Wang's performance activities in accordance with the agency contract, this did not constitute labor management in the sense of labor law but rather was a contractual obligation Wang was to perform as agreed. Second, Wang had relatively strong rights to negotiate and bargain over matters such as the method of revenue distribution. During the process of entering into the agreement with Beijing Mou Media Company, Wang focused on negotiating and bargaining over core content such as the revenue distribution ratio. The legal relationship between the parties reflected the characteristics of equal negotiation, and the agreed revenue distribution method of sharing profits was clearly different from a labor relationship. Third, from the perspective of the contract's purpose and content, the parties' original intention in cooperating was to use Beijing Mou Media Company's incubation to further enhance Wang's influence and popularity in art, performance, advertising, and image on self-media platforms, and then for Wang to independently participate in commercial activities to obtain corresponding advertising revenue, which would be distributed in accordance with the contract. The contract primarily included provisions on rights and obligations concerning agency matters, remuneration and revenue distribution, and liability for breach, and did not contain the essential elements of a labor contract.

In summary, the rights and obligations between Beijing Mou Media Company and its network anchor Wang did not conform to the characteristics of personal subordination, economic subordination, and organizational subordination between a worker and an employer required by labor management. Therefore, it should not be determined that a labor relationship existed as a matter of law.

Related Laws

Article 7 of the Labor Contract Law of the People's Republic of China
